protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist assessment, prescription and supply of hormonal contraception within the Hormonal Contraception Service. Service restricted to patients aged 17 years or over. The Service covers four types — 'the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), the combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring, the progestogen-only pill (POP), and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection)' (p5), plus consideration/provision of the emergency contraceptive pill as standard pharmacy care (p8, p11). Covers referral tiers (urgent referral within 24 hours; prompt referral within 1 to 2 weeks; STI symptoms urgent assessment within 1 to 2 days), key points (mandatory consultation, LARC discussion, STI resources and testing), patient history and sexual/social history, STI risk, examination (BP and BMI), pregnancy exclusion ('reasonably certain' criteria), notes on specific population groups (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, young people under 18, sexual and domestic/family violence, transgender/non-binary/sexually diverse people, women over 50), method selection per Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception, method-specific eligibility and 'Refer when' UKMEC Category 3 and 4 lists for combined hormonal contraception, POP and DMPA, confirm management (UKMEC 3/4 must not be prescribed), communication of the agreed management plan, general advice and patient resources, VTE/cancer risk information, STI and cervical screening advice, breast checks, clinical review intervals (1 month, 12 monthly, at least every 2 years), and referral options. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

inclusion.text: 'Service restricted to patients aged 17 years or over.'

'Patients are required to have a pharmacist consultation prior to hormonal contraception being prescribed, regardless of whether the patient is currently using the type of contraception requested. This includes: Clinical history taking regarding assessment for appropriate contraception; Examination, including blood pressure (BP) and body mass index (BMI) monitoring; Pregnancy exclusion.'

'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines. The patient history should consider:' age; sex (assigned at birth), gender, pronouns; purpose for seeking contraception at this time; previous contraceptive use (tolerability, adverse effects (including mood related symptoms), reason for cessation); menstrual history (last normal menstrual period; frequency / cycle; 'irregular cycle suggests underlying disorder (e.g., PCOS) and should be referred to a medical practitioner'; 'post-coital and inter-menstrual bleeding are red flags and warrant urgent referral to a medical practitioner'); pregnancy history (gravidity and parity; most recent delivery; breastfeeding history and current breastfeeding status); past medical history ('see UKMEC Category 3 and 4 conditions'; 'in particular, migraine with or without aura, history of venous thromboses (e.g., pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis), personal or family history of breast cancer, hypertension or other vascular disease'); 'last Cervical Screening Test (CST) – refer to medical practitioner if due for CST'; 'Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination status'; current medications (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse effects; significant family history, e.g., PCOS, endometriosis, contraceptive failure, breast/ovarian/endometrial or other hormone responsive cancers; smoking status and history (including vaping); illicit drug history.

Sexual (and social) history and STI risk: 'Start by using a warning phrase (to ensure the patient is aware of the topic and types of questions you may be asking) and confirm confidentiality'; 'Ask open questions about the patient's social background ...'; 'More specific questions can then be asked about risk behaviours, followed by questions around sexual practices if required (27). These include: Enquire when last sex was; Sex of partner(s); Was this unprotected or protected (i.e., was a condom used); When was the last episode of unprotected sex (consider provision of the emergency contraceptive pill if appropriate); Condom breakage? Withdrawal method?; Missed pills or contraceptive failure possibility?; How many episodes of unprotected sex since last normal menstrual period'. STI risk (18, 27, 28, 32): 'sexual contact history, including number of recent partners ...; risk behaviours including illicit and/or intravenous drug use, alcohol use; risk factors for STls (including STI history of current and/or recent partner/s if applicable); if there are there any concerns about symptoms of STIs – refer for urgent assessment (within 1 to 2 days) if symptoms present'.

'The pharmacist should measure BP and calculate BMI to determine the patient's suitability for their preferred contraceptive type, and to monitor potential impacts of contraception, including hypertension. BP should be measured in accordance with the National Heart Foundation of Australia Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults (33). A single elevated BP reading (systolic ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg) is not enough to classify a woman as hypertensive and a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation (33, 34).'

'Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception (35-37).' 'Health practitioners can be "reasonably certain" that a woman is not currently pregnant if any of one of the following criteria are met AND there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy:' (1) 'No intercourse since the start of last normal menstrual period, or since childbirth, abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or uterine evacuation for gestational trophoblastic disease'; (2) 'Correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception (barrier methods can be assumed to be reliable if used correctly in this context)'; (3) 'Commencing within the first 5 days of the onset of a normal (natural) menstrual period'; (4) 'Less than 21 days post partum'; (5) 'First 5 days after abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or uterine evacuation'; (6) 'No intercourse for > 21 days and have a negative urine pregnancy test (3, 8).'

The request is for one of the four types of hormonal contraception available in the Hormonal Contraception Service — 'the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), the combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring, the progestogen-only pill (POP), and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection)'. A request for a method not available in the Service (e.g., a LARC) requires referral (EXC-6); the emergency contraceptive pill may be supplied 'as per standard pharmacy care' in addition (p11).

steps.description: Gather information and assess patient's needs — 'An individualised assessment of contraceptive and sexual health needs and suitability for hormonal contraception and management within the Service should consider: patient history including sexual history; discussion of all available contraceptive options (including options not available in the Service that may be suitable); assessment of medical eligibility and contraindications; BP measurement and BMI; risk assessment for STIs.' Patient history (p6-7): age; sex (assigned at birth), gender, pronouns; purpose for seeking contraception at this time; previous contraceptive use (tolerability, adverse effects including mood related symptoms, reason for cessation); menstrual history (last normal menstrual period; frequency / cycle; 'irregular cycle suggests underlying disorder (e.g., PCOS) and should be referred to a medical practitioner'; 'post-coital and inter-menstrual bleeding are red flags and warrant urgent referral to a medical practitioner'); pregnancy history (gravidity and parity; most recent delivery; breastfeeding history and current breastfeeding status); past medical history ('see UKMEC Category 3 and 4 conditions'; 'in particular, migraine with or without aura, history of venous thromboses (e.g., pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis), personal or family history of breast cancer, hypertension or other vascular disease'); 'last Cervical Screening Test (CST) – refer to medical practitioner if due for CST'; 'Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination status'; current medications; drug allergies/adverse effects; significant family history, e.g., PCOS, endometriosis, contraceptive failure, breast/ovarian/endometrial or other hormone responsive cancers; smoking status and history (including vaping); illicit drug history. Sexual (and social) history (p8): warning phrase and confirm confidentiality; open questions about social background; risk behaviours and sexual practices — 'Enquire when last sex was; Sex of partner(s); Was this unprotected or protected (i.e., was a condom used); When was the last episode of unprotected sex (consider provision of the emergency contraceptive pill if appropriate); Condom breakage? Withdrawal method?; Missed pills or contraceptive failure possibility?; How many episodes of unprotected sex since last normal menstrual period'. STI risk (p8): 'sexual contact history, including number of recent partners ...; risk behaviours including illicit and/or intravenous drug use, alcohol use; risk factors for STls ...; if there are there any concerns about symptoms of STIs – refer for urgent assessment (within 1 to 2 days) if symptoms present'. Sexual/domestic violence and assault disclosures: 'Have appropriate referral options ... ALL sexual assault patients should be offered referral to a medical practitioner as soon as possible ... Consider a safety plan ... Consider mandatory reporting depending on scenario (e.g., Child Abuse Report Line – CARL) (31).'

steps.description: Exclude pregnancy — 'Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception (35-37).' 'Health practitioners can be "reasonably certain" that a woman is not currently pregnant if any of one of the following criteria are met AND there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy:' (1) 'No intercourse since the start of last normal menstrual period, or since childbirth, abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or uterine evacuation for gestational trophoblastic disease'; (2) 'Correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception (barrier methods can be assumed to be reliable if used correctly in this context)'; (3) 'Commencing within the first 5 days of the onset of a normal (natural) menstrual period'; (4) 'Less than 21 days post partum'; (5) 'First 5 days after abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or uterine evacuation'; (6) 'No intercourse for > 21 days and have a negative urine pregnancy test (3, 8).' 'Pharmacists should ensure a comprehensive history is taken with explicit questioning regarding the risk of pregnancy with sexual activity, e.g., condom breakage, use of withdrawal method, would constitute a pregnancy risk. Consider need for pregnancy test – low threshold to perform urine beta human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) test. It may be appropriate to refer to a medical practitioner for a blood test for serum hCG levels ... If there is any doubt regarding whether the patient may be pregnant, even if a negative urine test is returned, hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed and the patient referred to a medical practitioner.' Managing a positive pregnancy test: 'Ask the patient what this means for them – how do they feel? Avoid using emotive language. Use a non-judgmental and non-directive approach – avoid congratulating the patient or assuming abortion. The patient should be urgently referred to their usual GP, Urgent Care Centre, or pregnancy advisory provider.'

gates.criterion: reasonably certain not currently pregnant — ANY ONE of the six printed criteria met (any_of) AND there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy (all_of)
no pregnancy risk from sexual activity (condom breakage, withdrawal method) (RF-4 / EXC-4)

no doubt about possible pregnancy — 'If there is any doubt ... even if a negative urine test is returned, hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed and the patient referred to a medical practitioner' (RF-21)
if a positive pregnancy test: non-judgmental counselling provided and patient urgently referred to usual GP, Urgent Care Centre, or pregnancy advisory provider (RF-20)

steps.description: Prescribe within the Service — 'The Hormonal Contraception Service allows for the prescription of four types of hormonal contraception - the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), the combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring, the progestogen-only pill (POP), and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection).' In addition, 'When was the last episode of unprotected sex (consider provision of the emergency contraceptive pill if appropriate)' (p8) and 'Emergency contraception should be considered in these (and all cases) and may be supplied as per standard pharmacy care, or the patient may be referred to an appropriate medical practitioner or health service for another method of emergency contraception e.g., insertion of a copper intrauterine device' (p11). COCP choice (p17): 'The COCP with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen that is well tolerated and able to provide acceptable menstrual cycle control for each patient should be chosen as first-line (15, 18). Low-dose estrogen pills (ethinylestradiol 35 micrograms or less) with levonorgestrel or norethisterone are considered the "gold standard" (15).' 'COCPs with a high estrogen dose (50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol or mestranol) ... are not permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' Age eligibility for combined hormonal contraception (p14): 'Patients aged 17 to 40 years: Eligible for the prescription of combined hormonal contraception (this includes initiation and continuation). Patients aged 41 to 50 years: Pharmacists may only prescribe continuation of existing combined hormonal contraception ... One original manufacturer's pack ... Do not initiate combined hormonal contraception in this age group.' Vaginal ring (p17): 'Patients that require assistance with insertion of a vaginal ring must be referred to a medical practitioner.' POP (p18): 'For patients who have a contraindication to estrogen in COCPs or have a preference for estrogen free contraception, POPs can be considered (8). Drospirenone provides more consistent suppression of ovulation than levonorgestrel or norethisterone and may provide better bleeding control (37, 50).' Elevated BP or BMI ≥ 35 do not contraindicate POP or DMPA initiation, but the patient should be referred for further investigation (EXE-5). DMPA (p19): 'DMPA may be the contraceptive of choice for individuals with contraindications to estrogen, those taking drugs that induce the CYP3A4 liver enzyme ... or if a discrete method of contraception is preferred with less user input required. DMPA cannot be immediately reversed ... DMPA is not a first-line option for adolescents or in perimenopausal women ... Consider an alternative method of contraception in individuals less than 25 years (certainly less than 18 years) and over 45 years requesting initiation of DMPA.' 'Pharmacists should discuss with patients, the increased risk of intracranial meningioma with prolonged use of DMPA.'

steps.description: Communicate the agreed management plan — 'Comprehensive counselling that covers adverse effects, instructions for use and patient expectations assists to promote effective and ongoing contraceptive use (52).' 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, UKMEC, and other relevant references, should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use (instructions for commencing; time to efficacy, and how long a secondary method of contraception must be used to avoid an unplanned pregnancy; deviation from schedule (a pill is missed, a DMPA injection is not administered at 12 weeks, or a new vaginal ring is inserted too late or removed before the 3-week interval); instructions on tailored regimens); emergency contraceptive options that are available in instances of contraceptive failure; how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment (the signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected; the importance of reporting new or worsening mood-related symptoms to the pharmacist and usual medical practitioner); when to return to the pharmacist for clinical review.' 'The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.' Also: 'Before prescribing hormonal contraception, pharmacists should discuss the use of long-acting reversible contraception (LARCs) with women seeking contraception, as per the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) recommendations'; 'Individuals accessing the Service should be provided with appropriate resources regarding sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and be advised to be tested if at risk or symptomatic'; 'Condoms should be provided at each consultation as required'; DMPA-specific: discuss 'the increased risk of intracranial meningioma with prolonged use of DMPA' and that 'DMPA cannot be immediately reversed, and women should be informed that there may be a delay of more than 1 year in the return of fertility after discontinuation (21)'.

steps.description: Clinical review — 'Clinical review with the pharmacist should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines and other relevant guidelines. Clinical review is recommended 1 month after initiation of new contraceptive method (the patient has no recent experience of taking that type of contraception) to screen for adverse effects including hypertension. Clinical review, including measurement of the patient's BP, is recommended at 12 monthly intervals (15, 19, 35, 49). Calculation of BMI should occur on the first presentation, and professional judgement exercised regarding whether BMI needs to be recalculated on subsequent presentations ... Patients taking a regular contraceptive should have a review with a medical practitioner or other appropriate health service at least every 2 years. Pharmacists should generally only prescribe (including repeats) a sufficient quantity of medicine for the period until the patient's next review.' DMPA reviews (p19): 'During each annual consultation, pharmacists should assess the user's risk factors for low BMD and cardiovascular disease (36). Women who wish to continue using DMPA should be reviewed by a medical practitioner every 2 years to assess any changes in benefits and potential risks of use (21).' Age-related review (p12): 'The choice of contraceptive should be reconsidered at age 50 and at menopause (3). Contraceptive use may be discontinued when the patient reaches 55 years of age, or earlier if menopause has occurred (48). For women over 50, menopause may be assumed after one year of amenorrhoea and contraception can be ceased at this time. For women aged between 40-50, it is recommended that contraception be continued for an additional year (2 years of amenorrhoea) (48).'

open_questions.topic: Criteria combinatorics are not printed as AND/OR keys
open_questions.observed: Inclusion INC-1 to INC-7 recorded as all_of (all are preconditions of the printed consultation requirement). Exclusions grouped into seven clusters: p4 urgent-24-hours any_of (EXC-1 to EXC-5), p4 prompt-1-to-2-weeks any_of (EXC-6 to EXC-11), p14/17 service-limit any_of (EXC-12 to EXC-14), p15-16 combined hormonal contraception refer-when any_of (EXC-15 to EXC-42), p18 POP refer-when any_of (EXC-43 to EXC-46), p19 DMPA refer-when any_of (EXC-47 to EXC-55), and the p20 UKMEC 3/4 rule as its own all_of (EXC-56). The document never prints an AND/OR key.
open_questions.why_unclear: Combinatorics derived from the bullet structure ('Urgent referral within ...' lists and method-specific 'Refer when:' tables) rather than stated; recorded here per spec rule 4.

open_questions.topic: No dose, strength, frequency or duration table for any treatment
open_questions.observed: TX-1 (combined oral contraceptive pill), TX-2 (combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring), TX-3 (progestogen-only pill), TX-4 (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection) and TX-5 (emergency contraceptive pill) have empty strength/dose fields. Dosing is delegated: 'Hormonal contraception must be prescribed in accordance with Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception (3)' (p12); 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, the UKMEC, and other relevant references' (p20). Route/frequency values that are printed (oral/daily pill taking, 12-weekly injection, 3-week ring interval) are transcribed from p5/p21.
open_questions.why_unclear: Inventing a regimen would breach the never-invent rule; regimens must come from the cited external guidelines (see hugh_to_confirm).

open_questions.observed: 'A single elevated BP reading (systolic ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg)' (p9); 'Consistently elevated systolic blood pressure 140 mmHg or higher, or diastolic blood pressure 90 mmHg or higher' (p15); POP/DMPA 'If BP is elevated (systolic ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg)' (p18, p20).
open_questions.why_unclear: Each printed rule is an OR of two thresholds, so a single parameter/value structure would drop a limb; RF-8, RF-33, RF-72 and RF-73 are recorded with structured null and exact printed wording for the engine to surface as a judgement prompt.

open_questions.topic: No emergency referral tier printed — referral.emergency is empty
open_questions.observed: The guideline prints only 'Urgent referral within 24 hours' and 'Prompt referral within 1 to 2 weeks' (p4), 'urgent assessment (within 1 to 2 days)' for STI symptoms (p8-9) and 'urgently referred' for a positive pregnancy test (p10). There is no 'call 000' / emergency department tier anywhere in the 29 pages.
open_questions.why_unclear: Empty array is genuine (spec allows it), but a prescribing-support engine may expect a 000 tier as in other SA CPGs — see hugh_to_confirm.

open_questions.topic: STI trigger: urgent 24-hour referral versus 'hormonal contraception may still be provided'
open_questions.observed: p4 lists 'The patient has symptoms or is suspected to have an STI' under 'Urgent referral within 24 hours' with the parenthetical '(hormonal contraception may still be provided by the pharmacist)'. p22 reinforces eligibility: 'They are still eligible for the Hormonal Contraception Service.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Both readings recorded: EXC-5/RF-5 keep the 24-hour referral tier; EXE-2 records the explicit exception that supply may continue. The engine needs to know whether to hold supply pending referral.

open_questions.observed: p4: 'Urgent referral within 24 hours: The patient is younger than 17 years of age.' p11: 'Patients younger than 17 are to be confidentially referred to a sexual health clinic or medical practitioner (note: the minimum age eligible for this service is 17 years, as the age of sexual consent in South Australia is 17 years old).'
open_questions.why_unclear: Two referral frames for the same fact (urgent tier vs confidential referral, destinations differ); both transcribed (RF-1 REFER_URGENT, RF-22 REFER) without reconciling.

open_questions.topic: BMI ≥ 35 and hypertension: referral tier versus POP/DMPA exceptions
open_questions.observed: p4 prompts referral within 1 to 2 weeks for 'body mass index (BMI) ≥ 35' and 'hypertension'; p15-16 lists them again as UKMEC 3/4 refer-when conditions for combined hormonal contraception; yet p18/p20 state 'elevated BP is not a contraindication for commencing POP/DMPA' and 'BMI ≥ 35 is not a contraindication for commencing POP/DMPA' — initiation permitted with concurrent referral for further investigation.
open_questions.why_unclear: Both readings recorded (EXC-7/EXC-8/EXC-19/EXC-21 versus EXE-5); which method is being prescribed changes the outcome, so the engine must branch on method.

open_questions.topic: UKMEC criteria are external to this document
open_questions.observed: 'The preferred contraceptive type is contraindicated or not appropriate (UKMEC 3 or 4)' (p4); 'A hormonal contraception that is classified as UKMEC category of 3 or 4 ... must not be prescribed, administered or dispensed' (p20); the guideline prints only method-selected 'Refer when' subsets (p15-16, p18, p19) and cites 'UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC) 2016 (14)' and 'UKMEC Calculator (16)' (p25).
open_questions.why_unclear: The full UKMEC 2016 table is not reproduced, so EXC-15 to EXC-56 cannot be fully evaluated from this document alone; confidence in individual rows is 'high' (they are verbatim) but coverage is partial.

open_questions.topic: Mapping of the document's own urgency wording to action/severity
open_questions.observed: 'Urgent referral within 24 hours' → REFER_URGENT/high; 'Prompt referral within 1 to 2 weeks' → REFER/medium; 'urgent assessment (within 1 to 2 days)' → REFER_URGENT/high; 'as soon as possible' (sexual assault) → REFER_URGENT/high; 'should be referred'/'must be referred' → REFER/medium; 'reconsidered at age 50'/'should be advised to see' → REVIEW_GP/low; age restriction, initiation ban, non-permitted formulations and UKMEC 3/4 → NOT_ELIGIBLE.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document prints its own tiers but no numeric severity; mapping recorded so it can be re-checked (see also impetigo/wound sibling mappings).

open_questions.observed: referral.provenance uses page 4 (first page of the referral section); STI symptom tiers are p8-9, positive pregnancy test p10, under-17/capacity p11, method-specific refer-when lists p15-19, and referral options p24.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; range recorded here.

open_questions.observed: 'Major surgery with prologed immobilisation' (p15); 'Significant lifestyle and/or medical risk factorsfor osteoporosis' (p19); 'risk factors for STls' / 'prevent STls' (p8, p22); unclosed parenthesis in 'Known thrombogenic mutations (e.g., factor V Leiden ...' (p15); '50micrograms' (p17); reference 9 prints '& MS, Dohme (MSD)'; reference 12 prints 'The Australasian Society for HIV VHaSHMA'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed as printed with a note in brackets; may be source errors or extraction artefacts. No correction applied (never-invent rule).

open_questions.topic: No upper age bound; age-band rules instead
open_questions.observed: 'Service restricted to patients aged 17 years or over' (p3); combined hormonal contraception: 'Patients aged 17 to 40 years: Eligible ...' and 'Patients aged 41 to 50 years: ... Do not initiate' (p14); 'The choice of contraceptive should be reconsidered at age 50 and at menopause' (p12).
open_questions.why_unclear: age_bounds recorded as min_years 17, max_years null because the document prints no absolute maximum; age-band branching lives in EXC-12/EXE-6/RF-25/RF-26.

open_questions.topic: Emergency contraceptive pill has no product detail
open_questions.observed: 'consider provision of the emergency contraceptive pill if appropriate' (p8); 'Emergency contraception should be considered in these (and all cases) and may be supplied as per standard pharmacy care, or the patient may be referred ... e.g., insertion of a copper intrauterine device' (p11).
open_questions.why_unclear: No agent (levonorgestrel/ulipristal), strength, dose, timing window or route is printed anywhere; TX-5 fields left empty.

open_questions.topic: Mandatory reporting threshold is scenario-dependent and undefined
open_questions.observed: 'Consider mandatory reporting depending on scenario (e.g., Child Abuse Report Line – CARL) (31)' (p8); 'Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns relating to a request for contraception and report to the Child Abuse Report Line accordingly' (p11).
open_questions.why_unclear: No criteria, decision tree or documentation standard is printed; notifiable.required recorded as true with the CARL condition only — the engine cannot auto-trigger this.

open_questions.topic: DMPA age considerations are advisory, not exclusions
open_questions.observed: 'Consider an alternative method of contraception in individuals less than 25 years (certainly less than 18 years) and over 45 years requesting initiation of DMPA' and 'DMPA is not a first-line option for adolescents or in perimenopausal women' (p19).
open_questions.why_unclear: 'Consider an alternative' is weaker than 'Refer when'; RF-70 recorded with action REFER and confidence medium rather than as an exclusion.

open_questions.topic: Suspected VTE has counselling text but no printed action
open_questions.observed: Counselling covers 'when to seek further care and/or treatment (the signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected ...)' (p21), but no escalation destination or timeframe is stated for a suspected VTE event.
open_questions.why_unclear: RF-75 mapped to REVIEW_GP/medium by inference; structured null so the engine surfaces it as a judgement prompt. The document does print VTE risk context (p22) without an action.

open_questions.topic: Quantity to supply has no pack size or duration
open_questions.observed: 'Pharmacists should generally only prescribe (including repeats) a sufficient quantity of medicine for the period until the patient's next review' (p23); the only concrete quantity printed is 'One original manufacturer's pack' for combined hormonal contraception continuation at ages 41 to 50 (p14).
open_questions.why_unclear: No number of months/cycles/packs is stated for the routine case (reviews are 1 month then 12 monthly); quantity_to_supply fields carry the printed statements only.

open_questions.topic: Permitted COCP formulations depend on an external table containing non-permitted products
open_questions.observed: 'The COCPs available in Australia and for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service are listed in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Formulations of combined hormonal contraception table (35). NB: This table does contain high estrogen COCPs (50micrograms of ethinylestradiol or mestranol) which are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' (p17)
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not reprint the permitted list; the pharmacist must filter the external table against RF-55/EXC-13 before prescribing.

open_questions.topic: LARC discussion requirement has no documentation standard
open_questions.observed: 'Before prescribing hormonal contraception, pharmacists should discuss the use of long-acting reversible contraception (LARCs) with women seeking contraception, as per the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) recommendations. See Long Acting Reversible Contraception (LARC) - Consensus Statement (MSD) for further information (9). Referral to a medical practitioner is required if the patient requests a form of contraception not available in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' (p5)
open_questions.why_unclear: LARC is outside the Service, so the discussion is a soft prerequisite with no printed checklist, recording requirement or pass/fail state.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Product-level prescribing data for the four Service methods — COCP agents (lowest effective dose, ethinylestradiol 35 micrograms or less with levonorgestrel or norethisterone 'gold standard'), vaginal ring product/strength, POP agents (levonorgestrel, norethisterone, drospirenone), DMPA product strength/dose/volume and 12-weekly schedule — from Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception, AMH and FSRH guidance.
